reasoning: I looked for any defense between the GitHub release metadata and the DMG being handed to the user, and found none that holds up against someone who controls the release. (1) Source: the tag, asset URL, size and checksums asset all come from the releases/latest JSON (UpdateChecker.swift:159-196). The SHA comes from a sibling asset in the same release, fetched with `try?` at :186, so a missing or unparseable checksums file leaves dmgSHA256 nil. (2) Sink: at :265 the DMG is moved into ~/Downloads, and at :275 it is revealed in Finder. The size check (:252-258) and the hash check (:259-264) only compare against values from that same release, and the hash check is skipped when there is no checksum. isAllowedDownloadURL (:282-288) only pins the host to GitHub, and GitHub is where the attacker publishes. (3) Missing mitigation: HTTPClient.swift:71 is a plain session.download. Searching Sources/ and Resources/ for quarantine or LSFileQuarantineEnabled finds nothing, and entitlements.plist:14-15 sets app-sandbox false. So the file never gets com.apple.quarantine, and the comment at :267-274 relying on Gatekeeper is not backed by code. UpdateChecker never checks a code signature or team ID, and no key outside the release (for example an EdDSA key like Sparkle uses) exists. The attacker does need to be able to publish a release, which is the REACHABILITY lens's call. Under DEFENSES, nothing in the code stops the attack once that is possible.
